name: Question 7
problem:
Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following are orthogonal sets?

I. $U=\{Q([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]),Q([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}])\}$

II. $V=\{Q([\begin{aligned}-1 \\ \sqrt{5} \\ -2\end{aligned}]),Q([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}]),Q([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}])\}$

III. $W=\{Q([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]),Q([\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2\end{aligned}])\}$
worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as 

$\,$ $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\},\,$ $\{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})\},\,$ and $\,\{Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})\}.$

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$

- $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]=-4+25=21\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the Set $V,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ \sqrt{5} \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}]=0+2\sqrt{5}-2\sqrt{5}=0,\,✓ \\ Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ \sqrt{5} \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=-2+0-2=-4.\,\times  \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0+0+\sqrt{5}=\sqrt{5}\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $W,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=-10+10=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$W$ only".

html:
Question 7
?

Let Q be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following are orthogonal sets?

  1. U={Q([25]),Q([−25])}
  2. V={Q([−15−2]),Q([025]),Q([201])}
  3. W={Q([25]),Q([−52])}
a
V and W only
b
W only
c
V only
d
U and W only
e
U,V, and W
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since Q is orthogonal, we have that Q(x)⋅Q(y)=x⋅y for any vectors x and y.

Let's denote the elements of U,W, and V respectively as

{Q(u1),Q(u2)}, {Q(v1),Q(v2),Q(v3)}, and {Q(w1),Q(w2)}.

The sets U,V, and W are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

  • Q(u1)⋅Q(u2)=0.

  • Q(v1)⋅Q(v2)=0,Q(v1)⋅Q(v3)=0,Q(v2)⋅Q(v3)=0.

  • Q(w1)⋅Q(w2)=0.

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

  • For the set U, we get Q(u1)⋅Q(u2)=u1⋅u2=[25]⋅[−25]=−4+25=21≠0.× So, U is not an orthogonal set.

  • For the Set V, notice that Q(v1)⋅Q(v2)=v1⋅v2=[−15−2]⋅[025]=0+25−25=0,✓Q(v1)⋅Q(v3)=v1⋅v3=[−15−2]⋅[201]=−2+0−2=−4.×v2⋅v3=[025]⋅[201]=0+0+5=5≠0.× So, V is not an orthogonal set.

  • For the set W, we get Q(w1)⋅Q(w2)=w1⋅w2=[25]⋅[−52]=−10+10=0.✓ So, the set W is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "W only".
